lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- When the Deadline Moves
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Gustavo Marinho de Carvalho | Lesson 3 -- When the Deadline Moves

listenings.text: Here is something people learn late, and usually the hard way. When a date slips, the damage almost never comes from the delay itself. It comes from how the other side finds out. If they hear it from you, on the day you know, a moved deadline is a piece of information and everybody adjusts. If they find out on the day the work was due, the same delay becomes something else entirely. It stops being about the calendar and it starts being about whether they can trust what you tell them. That is a much more expensive problem, and it lasts much longer. So the rule is short. The moment you know, they know. You do not need a solution ready, and you do not need to explain everything. You need one sentence saying what has changed, one saying what you are doing about it, and one asking what they need from you.

A quick warning about a sentence I misread for two years. When a British colleague looks at your plan and says that it might be a bit tight, that is not a small doubt and it is not encouragement. It is a no, delivered in the politest possible way, and everybody in the room except me understood it immediately. The same thing happens with I am not sure that would work, and with we could possibly look at that. All three mean the answer is no, or at least not like that. This is not people hiding what they think. It is a different setting on the same dial, and once you know the setting you can read it perfectly. The practical move is simple. When you hear one of those sentences, do not thank them and move on. Ask a direct question. What would need to change for this to work? You will get a straight answer, and they will be glad you asked.
